Name: Policy and procedures
Parameter values: Reviewed every year and after a significant change
How it works here: Access rules are written in the access control policy (Phase 3)
Why: Baseline control. One owner writes, approves and follows it

Name: Account management
Parameter values: Account types: app user, AWS administrator, code host owner, deploy role
How it works here: Invite-only accounts, created, changed and removed by the owner, and reviewed every quarter
Why: Applies in full. The quarterly review is the open part (D-022)

Name: Automated system account management
How it works here: Account actions run through one script
Why: A script is enough at this size

Name: Automated temporary and emergency account management
How it works here: No temporary or emergency accounts exist. Temporary passwords on new accounts expire in 7 days
Why: Nothing to manage. Comes back if temporary accounts are ever created

Name: Disable accounts
Parameter values: Accounts with no sync for 180 days are flagged for the owner at the quarterly review. Nothing is disabled or deleted automatically, and the owner checks with the person first
How it works here: Checked as part of the quarterly access review
Why: Users are family and friends who may pause for months, so automatic disabling would lock them out without adding much protection

Name: Automated audit actions
How it works here: Account-level audit trail records administrator account changes
Why: Applies in full, not yet in place

Name: Inactivity logout
Parameter values: No idle logout in the app. Tokens: 1 hour, refresh 30 days
How it works here: The device's own screen lock guards an idle session, and users can lock the app or sign out at any time
Why: The app leaves idle protection to the device by design. Keeping a phone locked is the user's responsibility, and the owner accepts the remaining risk (D-031)

Name: Disable accounts for high-risk individuals
Parameter values: Within 24 hours of learning of the risk
How it works here: The owner disables the account and signs it out of every device
Why: Fits a small group, because the owner knows each user personally

Name: Access enforcement
How it works here: Every route requires a valid token, and the user ID comes only from that token
Why: The core access rule

Name: Information flow enforcement
How it works here: The Content Security Policy limits where the app can send data to its own origin and the sign-in service
Why: Stops injected code from sending data elsewhere

Name: Separation of duties
How it works here: Pull request with self-review checklist, automated checks, a deploy notice, and a changelog users can see
Why: One person can't separate duties. These checks make changes visible instead

Name: Least privilege
How it works here: Separate identities for administration and deployment, with narrower deploy permissions planned
Why: Applies in full. Narrowing deploy rights is the open part (R-05)

Name: Authorize access to security functions
Parameter values: Security functions: AWS administration, code host settings, deploy role
How it works here: Only the owner holds these
Why: Applies, not yet verified

Name: Non-privileged access for nonsecurity functions
How it works here: Root isn't used for daily work, and the owner uses the app with a normal user account
Why: Applies, not yet verified

Name: Privileged accounts
How it works here: One AWS administrator identity, and no long-lived access keys on the owner's computer
Why: Applies, not yet verified

Name: Review of user privileges
How it works here: Part of the quarterly access review
Why: D-022 sets the frequency

Name: Log use of privileged functions
How it works here: Administrator actions go to the account-level audit trail
Why: Applies in full, not yet in place

Name: Prohibit non-privileged users from executing privileged functions
How it works here: The API has no administrator routes. Administration happens only through AWS
Why: True by design

Name: Unsuccessful logon attempts
Parameter values: Provider default: after 5 failed attempts, a 1-second lockout that doubles with each further failure, up to about 15 minutes. It resets after a successful sign-in or 15 minutes without attempts. The same applies to MFA codes
How it works here: AWS Cognito slows repeated failed sign-ins and MFA codes. There's no permanent lockout
Evidence: AWS Cognito developer guide, read 2026-11-05. AWS says the behavior may change. To confirm in Phase 5
Why: No setting to tune. A temporary lockout fits, because a permanent one would let anyone lock a user out by guessing, and MFA is also required

Name: System use notification
How it works here: No sign-in banner. The invitation email and setup screens explain the service
Why: The usual banner is a government system warning about monitoring. This private service has no legal need for one, and privacy terms come in Phase 6

Name: Device lock
Parameter values: Administrator devices: lock on idle. App: no idle lock, and Lock now is available
How it works here: Administrator devices are locked by the owner's settings. Users' phones rely on their own lock
Why: The owner doesn't manage users' phones, so the phone's lock and the app's Lock now stand in. A user who leaves a phone unlocked is an accepted risk (D-031), and user guidance will say so (PRV-01)

Name: Pattern-hiding displays
How it works here: Phone and computer lock screens hide what was on screen
Why: Built into the devices

Name: Session termination
How it works here: Sessions end when tokens expire, and the owner can sign a user out of every device
Why: Long refresh suits a phone app. MFA and device lock offset it

Name: User-initiated logouts
How it works here: Users can sign out or lock the app from Settings, which clears the unlocked key from the device
Why: Not in the moderate baseline. Added because the app has no idle lock, so a user's own lock and sign-out matter more

Name: Permitted actions without identification or authentication
Parameter values: Only loading public app files and the demo
How it works here: Nothing with user data works without sign-in
Why: Public files hold no user data

Name: Remote access
Parameter values: Allowed routes: the app over HTTPS, AWS console and CloudShell, code host
How it works here: All access is remote. There's no office network
Why: Applies in full. Stronger administrator sign-in is the open part (R-01)

Name: Monitoring and control
How it works here: Audit trail plus a monthly log review
Why: Applies in full, not yet in place

Name: Protection of confidentiality and integrity using encryption
How it works here: HTTPS everywhere, with content also encrypted before it leaves the device
Why: Encryption does double duty here

Name: Managed access control points
How it works here: Users come in through one CDN and API. Administrators come in through AWS and the code host
Why: Few entry points, all managed

Name: Privileged commands and access
How it works here: Administrator commands run in CloudShell
Why: Applies, not yet verified

Name: Wireless access
How it works here: The service runs no wireless network. AWS manages its facilities, and wireless use on personal devices is protected by HTTPS
Why: No organization wireless exists

Name: Authentication and encryption
How it works here: Same as AC-18
Why: No organization wireless exists

Name: Disable wireless networking
How it works here: Same as AC-18
Why: No organization wireless exists

Name: Access control for mobile devices
Parameter values: Administrator phone only. Users' own phones aren't managed
How it works here: Passcode, auto-lock and automatic updates on the owner's phone
Why: Users' phones are theirs, so encryption before upload is what protects data leaving them

Name: Full device or container-based encryption
How it works here: Full disk encryption on the computer, and device encryption on the phone

Name: Use of external systems
Parameter values: External systems: suppliers, and users' own devices
How it works here: Suppliers are assessed in Phase 5. The owner's devices follow END-01
Why: Applies. The whole service runs on external systems

Name: Limits on authorized use
How it works here: No staff use outside systems on the organization's behalf
Why: Written for staff using outside systems. Comes back with trigger T-06

Name: Portable storage devices, restricted use
How it works here: No organization data is kept on portable storage, apart from offline recovery keys
Why: Written for staff and organization data. Comes back with trigger T-06

Name: Information sharing
How it works here: Users can't share records with each other. Each user reaches only their own records
Why: No sharing feature exists. Comes back if one is added

Name: Publicly accessible content
How it works here: Deployed files hold no user data, the demo uses made-up data, and public documents are checked for sensitive items before each commit
Why: This public repository makes the control real. Writing the check into policy is the open part
